new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's penultimate record (StressTyp2 via Horton 1949:18 = par. 18; SPA 1979 paraphrase of pp. 10-14) and now verified first-hand in Horton's own words, but the 'fixed-strict' coding is too strong: Horton states that verbs carry main stress on the root-initial syllable and 'retain that stress through all their forms and compounds', with the penult of long verb forms receiving only secondary stress, and that deverbative nouns usually keep root-syllable stress; penult is the default for nouns and other words and the target of the listed verb departures (subjunctive, enclitics, long vowel-verbs, remote past). new_statements.rule_in_words: One main stress per word. Base principle penultimate (nouns 'in the majority of cases', polysyllabic nouns 'usually', other words, and monosyllabic roots, which throw stress onto the prefix = penult). Verbs are the systematic modification: main stress sits on the first syllable of the (typically disyllabic) root and is retained through all derived forms and compounds, so in long verb forms the main stress is NOT penultimate (the penult then takes a secondary stress); listed departures pull verb stress back to a penult (subjunctive: penult of the derived form; enclitics such as -nga: penult of the whole word; vowel-verbs of more than two syllables and remote-past forms tend to penult; verb + coalesced vowel-demonstrative: penult of the resulting word). Deverbative nouns usually, but not invariably, keep the root-syllable stress of the parent verb; ideophones irregular. Stressed syllable described with short vowel and high tone in deverbatives (par. 363).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Par. 22 'Secondary stress occurs: a. Verb forms of more than [.] syllables after the main stress show a secondary stress on the penult: vahindukilile b. When the main stress of such a verb is drawn forward as in 21. a., b[.] normally stressed syllable retai[n]s a secondary stress: katwahan j i ki 1 ileko'; nouns: '[.] a secondary stress: kapopolwe.li, litengulula b. Compound nouns have a secondary stress on [.]'; 'of more than three syllables, whose stress is drawn forward as under 27, have a secondary [stress]'.
new_statements.exceptions: 'Departure from the principle of root-syllable stress is found in the following instances: a. In the subjunctive, where the stress shifts to the penult of a derived form: -tambuka (walk), ngutambuke[.]'; '[.]tive enclitic -nga, 394), where the stress is drawn onto the penult of the word : nguhane (give me), nguhaneco[.]'; 'f. Vowel-verbs of more than two syllables tend to take the stress on the penult.'; '[.] not vowel-stems also tend to stress the penult in the remote past; e.g., vangulwezele'; 'vowel-demonstrative coalesces with the verb, the main stress is drawn to the penultimate of the resulting [.]'; '25. Polysyllabic nouns are usually stressed on the penult. There are some exceptions'; deverbatives 'usually, but not invariably, retain the root-syllable stress of the parent form: kapopolwe ji'; 'ideophones are somewhat of a law to themselves'.
new_statements.identity_note: Horton 1949 describes Luvale (Lwena, Lovale; Bantu K14) as spoken in the then Balovale district of Northern Rhodesia (Zambia) and adjacent Angola; no copy opened to confirm the dialect basis.
